-- Check if delivery_order_id links to orders table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_deliveries, COUNT(DISTINCT d.delivery_order_id) AS distinct_order_ids FROM deliveries d

q2.sql:
-- Check how many deliveries have no matching order in orders table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unmatched_deliveries FROM deliveries d LEFT JOIN orders o ON d.delivery_order_id = o.delivery_order_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL

q3.sql:
-- Check how many orders have no matching delivery
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unmatched_orders FROM orders o LEFT JOIN deliveries d ON o.delivery_order_id = d.delivery_order_id WHERE d.delivery_id IS NULL

q4.sql:
-- Check if some delivery_order_ids have multiple deliveries (one order, multiple delivery attempts?)
SELECT delivery_order_id, COUNT(*) AS delivery_count FROM deliveries GROUP BY delivery_order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 LIMIT 20

q5.sql:
-- Check the distribution of delivery_status values
SELECT delivery_status, COUNT(*) AS cnt, ROUND(COUNT(*) * 100.0 / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER(), 2) AS pct FROM deliveries GROUP BY delivery_status

q6.sql:
-- Check if driver_id has nulls and what that means - are there deliveries without assigned drivers?
SELECT delivery_status, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(CASE WHEN driver_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_driver_count FROM deliveries GROUP BY delivery_status

q7.sql:
-- Check how many delivery_order_ids have more than 2 deliveries
SELECT delivery_order_id, COUNT(*) AS delivery_count FROM deliveries GROUP BY delivery_order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 LIMIT 10

q8.sql:
-- Check the max delivery_distance and see if there are outliers
SELECT MIN(delivery_distance_meters) AS min_dist, MAX(delivery_distance_meters) AS max_dist, AVG(delivery_distance_meters) AS avg_dist, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY delivery_distance_meters) AS median_dist FROM deliveries WHERE delivery_distance_meters > 0

q14.sql:

-- Check if order_id, payment_order_id, and delivery_order_id are the same
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) as total_rows,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) as distinct_order_ids,
    COUNT(DISTINCT payment_order_id) as distinct_payment_order_ids,
    COUNT(DISTINCT delivery_order_id) as distinct_delivery_order_ids,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_id = payment_order_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as order_equals_payment,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_id = delivery_order_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as order_equals_delivery,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_id = payment_order_id AND order_id = delivery_order_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as all_three_equal
FROM orders

orders.table_note: Each row records one food order with its status, financials, and timestamps across the order lifecycle. All three ID columns (order_id, payment_order_id, delivery_order_id) contain identical values, serving as the key to join with payments (via payment_order_id) and deliveries (via delivery_order_id).

database_note: The orders table records transaction events, linking to payments via payment_order_id and to deliveries via delivery_order_id. The payments table tracks financial transactions, while the deliveries table logs delivery attempts. These three tables form the core event chain. The stores table describes physical locations and links to hubs through hub_id. The hubs table defines distribution centers. The drivers table profiles personnel, connecting to deliveries via driver_id. The channels table lists sales platforms, joining orders through channel_id. Use orders as the central fact table. Join payments and deliveries to orders using their respective order ID columns. Connect stores to hubs via hub_id. Link drivers to deliveries via driver_id. Link channels to orders via channel_id. This structure separates transactional data from descriptive reference data, enabling clear analysis of sales, fulfillment, and logistics performance.
